name: Limit Public Release of Information
description: Limit the public release of technical information about the AI stack used in an organization's products or services. Technical knowledge of how AI is used can be leveraged by adversaries to perform targeting and tailor attacks to the target system. Additionally, consider limiting the release of organizational information - including physical locations, researcher names, and department structures - from which technical details such as AI techniques, model architectures, or datasets may be inferred.

name: Limit Model Artifact Release
description: Limit public release of technical project details including data, algorithms, model architectures, and model checkpoints that are used in production, or that are representative of those used in production.

name: Predictive AI Output Obfuscation
description: Reduce the fidelity and amount of information returned by predictive AI inference endpoints to make model discovery, extraction, replication, and black-box adversarial-example optimization more difficult. Limit outputs to those required by the application. Depending on the use case, this may include withholding or reducing the precision of confidence scores, logits, class rankings, labels, embeddings, or additional model metadata.

name: Predictive AI Model Hardening
description: Design and train predictive AI models to maintain intended performance when presented with adversarial examples. Adversarial examples may include digitally perturbed inputs or physical countermeasures intended to cause misclassification, missed detection, or another attacker-selected prediction. Robustness techniques may include adversarial training, robust model architectures, defensive distillation, and certified robustness methods.

name: Limit AI Service Query Volume and Rate
description: Limit the number and rate of requests that users can submit to an AI service. Apply limits by user, API key, tenant, device, or other authenticated identity. Use short-term rate, burst, and concurrency limits together with longer-term usage quotas. Query limits can increase the time and cost required to extract model information, optimize adversarial inputs, discover system behavior, verify attacks, or overwhelm a service. Monitor for attempts to evade limits through distributed requests, account rotation, or stolen credentials. Query limits may not protect against attacks that require few requests or are performed against an offline model.

name: Control Access to AI Models and Data at Rest
description: Establish access controls on internal model registries and limit internal access to production models. Limit access to training data only to approved users.

name: Predictive AI Ensembles
description: Use an ensemble of diverse predictive AI models to reduce reliance on a single model or model family and improve robustness against adversarial examples. Ensemble members should be sufficiently diverse, such as through different architectures, training procedures, features, or model families. Combine their predictions using an aggregation or adjudication method designed to prevent an adversarial example that evades one model from controlling the system's predictions.

name: Sanitize Training Data
description: Detect, quarantine, and remove or remediate poisoned data before it is used to train an AI model. Apply screening when datasets are acquired or updated, and before new data is incorporated into active learning workflows. Inspect data samples, annotations, and metadata for evidence of manipulation. Depending on the data and intended task, checks may include label inconsistencies, anomalous samples, unexpected shifts in source or class distributions, suspicious duplication or repeated patterns, and backdoor triggers. Compare findings with trusted dataset versions and combine automated screening with targeted review. Quarantine suspicious records while they are investigated. Remove malicious additions, correct affected labels or annotations, or restore data from a trusted version where appropriate. Repeat screening after remediation and before utilizing the dataset for training tasks. If affected data has already been used for training, identify the resulting models and evaluate whether retraining, rollback, or other corrective action is needed. Combine sanitization with Maintain AI Dataset Provenance and Validate AI Model. Tools that support screening and sanitizing training data include: - Adversarial Robustness Toolbox (ART) - Cleanlab

name: Validate AI Model
description: Evaluate AI models against defined functional requirements before deployment and throughout their operational lifecycle. Validate newly trained or acquired models and repeat evaluation after fine-tuning, model updates, or changes to the conditions in which the model is used. Use representative evaluation data and adversarial test cases appropriate to the model's capabilities and intended use. Test for unexpected behavior associated with poisoned training data, model tampering, backdoor triggers, adversarial inputs, and sensitive information disclosure. For generative models, include evaluations of susceptibility to prompt injection and jailbreaks, adherence to authorized instructions, and disclosure of information supplied in context or retained through training. Compare results against trusted baselines or previously evaluated model versions, and investigate significant regressions in performance or unexplained behavior. Use findings to inform model selection, remediation, deployment restrictions, or rollback, and repeat affected evaluations after corrective changes. During deployment, monitor for changes in model performance and use significant changes to trigger revalidation. Data or concept drift may result from legitimate changes in the operating environment and should be investigated alongside evidence of poisoning or tampering.

name: Predictive AI Multi-Sensor Fusion
description: Use independent physical sensors (ideally across multiple modalities or from several perspectives) to avoid relying on a single sensor that may be manipulated, obstructed, or disrupted by an adversary. Relevant sensors may include visible-light cameras, infrared cameras, depth sensors, radar, lidar, microphones, or other physical sensing systems. Corroborate observations across sensors so manipulation of one input source does not overly influence the model's predictions.

name: Predictive AI Input Restoration
description: Preprocess predictive AI inference inputs to remove, reduce, or disrupt adversarial perturbations before the inputs are evaluated by the model. Restoration methods may include denoising, compression, reconstruction, resampling, feature squeezing, randomized transformations, or other modality-appropriate preprocessing. Evaluate restoration methods against adaptive adversaries that account for the preprocessing operation.

name: Restrict Library Loading
description: Prevent abuse of library loading mechanisms in the operating system and software to load untrusted code by configuring appropriate library loading mechanisms and investigating potential vulnerable software. File formats such as pickle files that are commonly used to store AI models can contain exploits that allow for loading of malicious libraries.

name: Encrypt Sensitive Information
description: Encrypt sensitive data such as AI models to protect against adversaries attempting to access sensitive data.

name: Code Signing
description: Enforce binary and application integrity with digital signature verification to prevent untrusted code from executing. Adversaries can embed malicious code in AI software or models. Developers should also cryptographically sign SBOM and AIBOM components that track model or data provenance. Enforcement of code signing can prevent the compromise of the AI supply chain and prevent execution of malicious code.

name: Verify AI Artifacts
description: Verify the integrity and authenticity of AI artifacts before importing, loading, or deploying them. Artifacts may include model weights and checkpoints, datasets, tokenizers, model configurations, prompt templates, and agent configuration files. Verify the complete set of files used by the AI system, including supporting files that can alter model or agent behavior. Compare cryptographic hashes against expected values obtained from an authenticated publisher. Where digital signatures or signed manifests are available, verify that they cover the artifacts being used and were produced by an authorized signer. Do not rely solely on checksums distributed alongside an artifact through the same untrusted or compromised source. Pin approved artifacts to specific versions and cryptographic digests rather than relying on mutable names, tags, or download locations. Verify artifacts when they are acquired, transferred, or updated, and before they are loaded or interpreted. Successful verification establishes that an artifact matches a trusted reference or was signed by an accepted identity. It does not establish that the artifact is free of malicious code, poisoned data, backdoors, or harmful instructions. Combine artifact verification with Vulnerability Scanning and Validate AI Model.

name: Predictive AI Adversarial Input Detection
description: Detect and block digital or physical adversarial examples submitted to predictive AI models. Adversarial examples are inputs modified or constructed to cause misclassification, missed detection, excessive computation, or another attacker-selected behavior. Apply detection before model inference and monitor for input characteristics or query patterns associated with adversarial example generation, transfer attacks, or black-box optimization. Detection may use statistical tests, auxiliary models, consistency checks, input distribution analysis, or modality-specific adversarial example detectors.

name: Vulnerability Scanning
description: Vulnerability scanning is used to find potentially exploitable software vulnerabilities to remediate them. File formats such as pickle files that are commonly used to store AI models can contain exploits that allow for arbitrary code execution. These files should be scanned for potentially unsafe calls, which could be used to execute code, create new processes, or establish networking capabilities. Adversaries may embed malicious code in corrupt model files, so scanners should be capable of working with models that cannot be fully de-serialized. Model artifacts, downstream products produced by models, and external software dependencies should be scanned for known vulnerabilities.

name: AI Model Distribution Methods
description: Deploying AI models to edge devices can increase the attack surface of the system. Consider serving models in the cloud to reduce the level of access the adversary has to the model. Also consider computing features in the cloud to prevent gray-box attacks, where an adversary has access to the model preprocessing methods.

name: User Training
description: Educate AI model developers to on AI supply chain risks and potentially malicious AI artifacts. Educate users on how to identify deepfakes and phishing attempts.

name: Control Access to AI Models and Data in Production
description: Require users to verify their identities before accessing a production model. Require authentication for API endpoints and monitor production model queries to ensure compliance with usage policies and to prevent model misuse.

name: Generative AI Guardrails
description: Guardrails are safety controls placed between users, tools, and generative AI models to evaluate prompts, retrieved context, model outputs, and agent actions before they are accepted, executed, or shown to a user. They can help block, modify, or route unwanted content such as malicious code, malicious instructions, sensitive data, unsupported claims, policy-violating responses, or unsafe tool requests. Guardrails can be implemented using rule-based controls such as filters, allowlists, blocklists, regular expressions, schema validation, policy rules, and permission checks, or using AI-based techniques such as classifiers, LLM reviewers/judges, named entity recognition, groundedness checks, and task-adherence checks. They may be applied at multiple stages of a generative AI workflow, including input handling, prompt construction, retrieval, tool execution, model output review, and post-deployment monitoring. Examples of specific guardrail implementations include: - Input moderation: Screen user prompts for harmful content, prompt injection attempts, jailbreak attempts, sensitive data, off-topic requests, or inputs that exceed expected length or format. - Output moderation: Scan model responses before sending them to users for harmful content, PII, secrets, policy violations, unsupported claims, or unsafe code using classical scanners, classifiers, or a dedicated reviewer model . - System prompt and policy enforcement: Enforce system instructions, user roles, domain boundaries, response formats, and refusal policies before the model responds (See Generative AI Guidelines). - Tool and action guardrails: Validate tool calls, tool arguments, permissions, and tool outputs before execution or before results are returned to the model. Require human approval for high-impact, irreversible, privileged, or externally visible actions (See Human In-the-Loop for AI Agent Actions, Input and Output Validation for AI Agent Components). - Retrieval guardrails: Filter and validate retrieved documents before they are added to model context, including checks for untrusted sources, malicious instructions, irrelevant context, or sensitive data. - Groundedness and factuality checks: Compare model responses against trusted source material or approved knowledge bases to detect unsupported or hallucinated claims. - Sensitive data and secret protection: Detect, redact, or block personal information, credentials, tokens, proprietary data, system prompts, and other confidential information in prompts, retrieved context, tool outputs, and model responses. - Structured output validation: Enforce schemas, type checks, allowed values, and safe formats before model outputs are consumed by downstream systems Guardrails should be continuously evaluated, red-teamed, and updated as adversarial techniques evolve. Guardrail decisions should be logged (See AI Telemetry Logging and Monitoring) and observed failures should be systematically incorporated into updated policies, evaluation datasets, detection logic, prompts, and Generative AI Model Alignment.

name: Generative AI Guidelines
description: Guidelines are instructions, policies, and behavioral constraints provided to a generative AI model to direct it toward desired outputs and away from unsafe, unreliable, or policy-violating behavior. Guidelines can help reduce risks related to organization policy violations, brand damage, private data leakage, false or unsupported information, unsafe advice, and misuse of tools or external content. Guidelines can be implemented as system prompts, prompt templates, policy text appended to user prompts, or task-specific instructions included during prompt construction. They can define the system's goals, role, tone, allowed and disallowed behavior, domain boundaries, citation requirements, data-handling expectations, escalation criteria, and safety or security rules. Common prompt elements include: - Instructions to cite sources or identify when an answer is not supported by available context. - Instructions to treat external, retrieved, or user-provided content as untrusted data rather than authoritative sources. - Instructions to avoid revealing system prompts, hidden policies, credentials, private data, or other sensitive information. - Instructions to stay within the application's approved domain and refuse requests outside that scope. - Instructions to follow organization-specific policies, brand requirements, and regulated-domain restrictions. - Instructions to request human approval before proceeding with potentially unsafe, privileged, irreversible, or externally visible actions when untrusted content is in context (See Human In-the-Loop for AI Agent Actions). Guidelines should be tested, red-teamed, and updated as observed failures, prompt injection techniques, policy requirements, and application capabilities evolve. Guidelines are most effective when paired with Generative AI Guardrails that validate inputs, outputs, retrieved context, and tool use.

name: Generative AI Model Alignment
description: Generative AI Model Alignment is the process of training or fine-tuning a generative model to guide its output toward a set of human values, goals, or ethical principles. Desired principles can be in alignment with safety, security, content policies, and legal requirements, with goals such as removing harmful content or hallucinations, reducing biases, increasing predictability, and ensuring models do not have adverse societal consequences. In the context of agentic AI, alignment is about producing models that make decisions in support of the goals of the organization and individual users, with actions that remain in scope of the designated task, and designing agents that follow security standards, exhibit transparency in decision making, and operate within organizational boundaries. Common methods for aligning a generative model during training or fine-tuning include: - Reinforcement Learning from Human or AI Feedback (RLHF or RLAIF) - Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) - Targeted Safety Context Distillation - Instruction Tuning - Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) - Constitutional AI - Incoulation Prompting For agentic systems, alignment depends on the purpose of the agent, the tools available to the agent, and the levels of privileges and risks associated with tool calls. Standard alignment methods for LLMs can often be used in conjunction with domain-specific fine-tuning data, reward signals with examples of correct tool calls, or reinforcement learning based on interactions with a realistic environment. Examples of alignment methods specific to agentic AI are: - Trajectory Preference Optimization - Environment-Driven Reinforcement Learning - Reinforcement Learning with Execution Feedback (RLEF) - Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) Generative AI Model Alignment should be used in combination with Generative AI Guardrails and Generative AI Guidelines. Models should be continually evaluated for alignment and retrained or fine-tuned systematically to incorporate observed failure modes or updated policies. It is important to also consider that fine-tuning a model can remove previously learned alignments and should be undertaken with care and a comprehensive plan for testing the updated model for safety and security.

name: Maintain an AI Bill of Materials
description: Create and maintain an AI Bill of Materials (AI BOM) that identifies the components and dependencies used to build, evaluate, and operate an AI-enabled system. Include models and checkpoints, datasets, software packages, inference runtimes, container images, and agent configurations including system instructions and connected tools and data sources. For systems that use external AI services or agent tools, record the relevant providers, services, integrations, and available version identifiers. Record component identifiers, versions, sources, suppliers or publishers, and cryptographic digests. Capture dependency and derivation relationships, such as which base model and dataset versions produced a fine-tuned model. Link to supporting provenance, integrity-verification, and evaluation records rather than treating inclusion in the AI BOM as evidence of approval or safety. Generate or update the AI BOM when components are acquired, built, modified, or deployed. Retain version history and protect records from unauthorized modification. Identify gaps where upstream information or hosted-service version details are unavailable. Use the AI BOM to assess component changes, correlate security advisories and reports of compromised artifacts with deployed systems, and trace affected dependencies and derived models. Use these findings to prioritize investigation, replacement, rollback, or retraining. An AI BOM provides inventory and traceability. It does not establish that a listed component is authentic, unmodified, or free of malicious behavior. Combine it with Verify AI Artifacts, Maintain AI Dataset Provenance, and Validate AI Model.

name: AI Telemetry Logging and Monitoring
description: Implement logging and monitoring across the AI lifecycle to detect suspicious activity and support investigation. Capture security-relevant access, changes, and operations across data pipelines, model development, deployment, and connected systems. Preserve sufficient context to trace activity across components and identify coordinated behavior across accounts and access pathways. Tailor telemetry to each system's function, including relevant data and model versions, request and execution metadata, and operation results. For agentic systems, distinguish requested actions from those actually executed, using independent service records where available. Treat model-generated explanations and summaries as supporting context rather than authoritative evidence of execution. Monitor individual events and patterns over time for anomalous access, unauthorized changes, unusual usage, and unexpected model behavior or external actions. Correlate findings with related operational activity to guide investigation and response. Protect telemetry from unauthorized access, modification, or deletion, and monitor for gaps in coverage. Limit the collection of sensitive content through metadata, references, or redaction where these preserve investigative value, and apply appropriate retention controls.

name: Maintain AI Dataset Provenance
description: Maintain a detailed history of datasets used for AI applications. The history should include information about the dataset's source as well as a complete record of any modifications.

name: Manage AI Agent Service Access
description: Limit service AI agents--agents using independently assigned service or workload permissions--to explicitly authorized workflows. Agents may serve multiple users or act on requests, events, or schedules. Examples include service desk agents fulfilling support requests, operations agents restarting services after monitoring alerts, and reporting agents reading organizational data and publishing scheduled summaries. Apply least privilege to identities, roles, credentials, tools, and resources; permission to invoke an agent must not confer all its authority. Controls should include: - Dedicated Agent Identity: Use identifiable service or workload identities scoped to agent functions. Avoid unrestricted administrator accounts and broadly privileged identities shared across unrelated workflows. - Scoped Roles and Permissions: Use role-based or attribute-based controls to limit workflows to required operations and resources. Separate routine access from permission changes, credential management, security configuration, and deletion. - Workflow Initiation Authorization: Use trusted identity and authorization context to verify that requesters or triggers may initiate the specific workflow and affect its target resources. - Privilege Separation: Separate materially different workflows through distinct roles, credentials, or execution contexts. Prevent cross-workflow reuse of credentials or authorization state without explicit authorization. - Service Access Lifecycle Management: Limit elevated-access duration where supported, review grants as responsibilities change, and revoke unnecessary credentials or roles. Prevent unauthorized users and the agent itself from modifying permission configurations. An agent may perform operations unavailable directly to its requester, such as fulfilling an approved administrative request, but the requester must be authorized to initiate that workflow. Limit execution authority to the operations and resources needed to fulfill it. Use Enforce Access Controls for AI Agent Tools to enforce these restrictions when tools execute requests, and AI Agent Authority Expansion Controls to govern attempts to obtain additional authority during execution. Record the initiating user, application, service, event, or schedule, agent execution identity, authorization decision, and resulting activity through AI Telemetry Logging and Monitoring. Tools that may help implement these controls include: - Microsoft Entra ID: Provides service principals, managed identities, and application permissions for workloads. Workload identity federation supports authentication without stored application secrets where supported; Entra Agent ID provides agent-specific identities with directly assigned access. - Amazon Web Services IAM: Provides workload roles and temporary credentials scoped to required actions, resources, and conditions. IAM Access Analyzer supports permission review, policy validation, and policy generation from observed access.

name: Manage User-Delegated AI Agent Access
description: Limit user-delegated AI agents to explicitly authorized tasks and permissions. Apply the principle of least privilege so that the agent receives only the access required for its designated tasks. The user's permissions establish an upper bound; the agent should not automatically receive every permission available to that user. Controls should include: - Agent Identity and User Association: Bind an identifiable agent or application identity to the authorizing user. Distinguish both identities in access decisions and activity records. - Scoped Delegation: Limit operations, resources, and services to the required subset of user permissions, using read-only access where sufficient. Derive scope from trusted configuration or authorization mechanisms, not the agent's interpretation of requests. - Credential and Session Management: Use scoped, short-lived credentials where supported. Keep credentials outside model-visible context, isolate them across users' agents and sessions, and avoid broadly privileged shared accounts. - Access Lifecycle Management: Review delegation when tasks or user permissions change, and reflect removed user permissions in effective agent access. Expire or revoke credentials and sessions when delegation ends, the agent is decommissioned, or compromise is suspected. Enforce delegated permissions through the systems that provide access to tools and resources. Use Enforce Access Controls for AI Agent Tools to ensure that tool calls remain within the user's delegation, including when tools invoke downstream services. Use AI Agent Authority Expansion Controls to prevent the agent from autonomously obtaining additional authority outside its approved scope. Tools that may help implement these controls include: - Microsoft Entra ID: Supports user-delegated permissions, user and administrator consent, and token acquisition on behalf of users. Entra Agent ID provides agent-specific identities with delegated access bounded by granted permissions and the user's authorized access. - Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity: Provides agent workload identities and centralized credential management for AWS and third-party services. User-authorized OAuth integrations support access on behalf of users.

name: Enforce Access Controls for AI Agent Tools
description: Limit AI agent tool access to each caller's authorized, task-required operations and resources, including when tools are shared across agents, users, or tenants. Broader tool or backend privileges must not expand caller access. Enforce controls outside the model, in the tool implementation, MCP server, gateway, or underlying service. Enforce access controls outside the model: in the tool implementation, MCP server, access gateway, or underlying service. Controls should include: - Caller Authentication: Authenticate calling agents and derive identity, tenant, and delegation context from trusted authentication mechanisms, not model-generated arguments. - Request Authorization: Authorize each action on its target resource, separately controlling read, modify, and delete permissions. Deny requests when authorization cannot be established. - Delegated Access Enforcement: Enforce delegated permissions, trusted task restrictions, and tool policy through downstream calls. Use credentials scoped to each receiving service without expanding caller access. - Access Isolation: Isolate users' credentials, sessions, and authorization context. Select downstream credentials using verified caller context and prevent shared tool state from exposing another caller's resources. Tools that may help implement these controls include: - Open Policy Agent (OPA): Evaluates tool requests against caller identity, operations, resources, and trusted context. Tool services or gateways enforce the resulting least-privilege and caller-specific access decisions. - Cedar: Provides an authorization policy language and engine for evaluating caller actions on resources in context. Supports role- and attribute-based restrictions on tool operations and resources.

name: Human In-the-Loop for AI Agent Actions
description: Systems should require the user or another human stakeholder to approve AI agent actions before the agent takes them. The human approver may be technical staff or business unit SMEs depending on the use case. Separate tools, such as dedicated audit agents, may assist human approval, but final adjudication should be conducted by a human decision-maker. The security benefits from Human In-the-Loop policies may be at odds with operational overhead costs of additional approvals. To ease this, Human In-the-Loop policies should follow the degree of consequence of the task at hand. Minor, repetitive tasks performed by agents accessing basic tools may only require minimal human oversight, while agents employed in systems with significant consequences may necessitate approval from multiple stakeholders diversified across multiple organizations.

name: Restrict AI Agent Tool Invocation on Untrusted Data
description: Untrusted data can contain prompt injections that invoke an AI agent's tools, potentially causing confidentiality, integrity or availability violations. It is recommended that tool invocation be restricted or limited when untrusted data enters the LLM's context. The degree to which tool invocation is restricted may depend on the potential consequences of the action. Consider blocking the automatic invocation of tools or requiring user confirmation once untrusted data enters the LLM's context. For high consequence actions, consider always requiring user confirmation.

name: Memory Hardening
description: Memory Hardening protects persistent state used by AI agents, including saved preferences, episodic or semantic memories, conversation summaries, stored chat history, and agent-managed experience stores. Unlike guardrails that evaluate content during an interaction, memory hardening controls how durable agent state is created, modified, isolated, audited, and recovered. Apply the following controls throughout the memory lifecycle, from creation and use through deletion and recovery: - Enforce memory access controls: Authenticate memory operations and authorize them within the appropriate user, tenant, agent, and session scope. - Set strong memory security policies: Enforce limits on memory size and update frequency, validate memory integrity, and define retention and deletion policies. - Preserve memory provenance: Record the source of all memory updates and preserve a history with known good versions. Quarantine or roll-back suspicious records. - Audit and monitor memory operations: Audit security relevant reads and writes. Monitor for unusual update frequency and repeated self-authored updates. Content filtering and protections against malicious prompts may be provided by Generative AI Guardrails, but does not replace memory access control, isolation, provenance, integrity, or recovery. Open-source tools that implement memory hardening controls include OWASP Agent Memory Guard and Microsoft Agent Governance Toolkit. Memory management and persistence tooling such as Mem0, and LangGraph Persistence can also support aspects of memory hardening.

name: Segmentation of AI Agent Components
description: Define enforceable security boundaries around AI agent tools, data sources, identities, and execution environments. Mediate access through authenticated APIs, isolate code execution via containers or virtual machines, restrict filesystem and network access, and limit tool invocation rates. Build execution environments from clean base images for each run, and do not carry forward any operational state. These controls limit the ability of untrusted processes or compromised components to affect the broader system. When AI agents share infrastructure, isolate each agent's identity, credentials, state, storage, messaging, tools, and network access in order to prevent undesired agent-to-agent communication channels or coordination. Run the highest-risk workloads in network-isolated or air-gapped environments.

name: Input and Output Validation for AI Agent Components
description: Implement validation on inputs and outputs for the tools and data sources used by AI agents. Validation includes enforcing a common data format, schema validation, checks for sensitive or prohibited information leakage, and data sanitization to remove potential injections or unsafe code. Input and output validation can help prevent compromises from spreading in AI-enabled systems and can help secure the workflow when multiple components are chained together. Validation should be performed external to the AI agent.

name: Deepfake Detection
description: Apply deepfake detection algorithms against any untrusted or user-provided data, especially in impactful applications such as biometric verification, to block generated content. Detectors may use a combination of approaches, including: - AI models trained to differentiate between real and deepfake content. - Identifying common inconsistencies in deepfake content, such as unnatural facial movements, audio mismatches, or pixel-level artifacts. - Biometrics analysis, such blinking, eye movements, and microexpressions.

name: AI Red Team
description: Establish an AI red team responsible for conducting recurring, authorized, and threat-informed red-teaming exercises to identify and remediate vulnerabilities in AI-enabled systems before deployment and throughout operation. AI red-teaming simulates realistic adversary behavior to evaluate how attacks could affect the confidentiality, integrity, availability, safety, privacy, and mission performance of an AI-enabled system. Red-teaming exercises should consider the complete AI-enabled system, including models and data, agents (including memory and tools), data flows, decision processes, application logic, retrieval systems, identities and permissions, software dependencies, non-AI system components, infrastructure, user interfaces, and human workflows. An AI red team exercise can be organized into three phases: planning and scoping the exercise, executing the selected exercises, and assessing the results to guide reporting and remediation. 1. **Plan and Scope** - Document the system's intended use, deployment environment, users, sensitive data, connected resources, and potential consequences of failure or misuse. Diagram the system's components, trust boundaries, data flows, external services, human decision points, and training- and inference-time access points. - Establish rules of engagement covering authorized systems, accounts, data, techniques, test windows, resource limits, escalation procedures, evidence handling, and stop conditions. Plan destructive, privacy-invasive, or high-cost tests for isolated environments with appropriate safeguards. - Develop a threat model based on the system's operating environment and relevant adversary behavior. Define the adversary's objectives, access, knowledge, capabilities, resources, and constraints, and account for digital and physical attack paths and the role of human oversight. - Use ATLAS tactics, techniques, and procedures to identify relevant adversary behaviors and construct threat vectors. Prioritize them according to likelihood and severity of impact to the system. - Define success criteria and stopping conditions. Identify task-level metrics for effects on the AI capability and operational metrics for measuring impact to the overall system. 2. **Execute** - Conduct the selected exercises using manual and automated methods as appropriate. Automation can generate input variations, replay attack sequences, and evaluate responses at scale. Human testers can develop system-specific attacks, adapt to observed defenses, and investigate unexpected behavior. - Follow the rules of engagement and record attack activity, system responses, control behavior, deviations from the test plan, and evidence needed to evaluate the results. - Stop or escalate testing when predefined conditions are reached. After testing, remove test accounts, modified data, installed software, persistent instructions, and other exercise artifacts. 3. **Assess, Report, and Improve** - Evaluate the results against the defined task and operational metrics. Document successful and unsuccessful attacks, their consequences, observed control behavior, deviations from the test plan, and gaps in the threat model. - Report findings to the appropriate developers, defenders, operational teams, risk owners, and other stakeholders. - Assign findings to responsible owners, track remediation, and retest corrected systems. - Use demonstrated attacks to improve preventive controls, detection, incident response, and recovery. Where appropriate, convert confirmed failures into regression tests, evaluation datasets, detection logic, monitoring requirements, or deployment criteria. Red-teaming is a continuous process and should be repeated as the threat landscape evolves and when changes are made to the system, its components, intended use, or deployment environment. New threat intelligence, vulnerabilities, and test results should inform the scope and priorities of future exercises.

name: Limit AI Workload Resource Consumption
description: Limit the resources that an AI request, inference job, or agent workflow can consume. Set bounds on input size, batch size, execution time, memory, compute, and output size. Generative AI services should also limit context and output tokens. Agentic AI systems should limit iterations, retries, tool calls, parallel tasks, delegation depth, and downstream spending. Apply resource limits across the complete workflow because one request may initiate multiple model calls or external actions. Use timeouts, cost ceilings, circuit breakers, and safe termination conditions to prevent individual workloads from exhausting shared resources. These controls complement query-rate limits, which address large numbers of otherwise inexpensive requests.

name: AI Agent Authority Expansion Controls
description: Limit an AI agent's ability to autonomously acquire additional authorities that expand its effective permissions during execution. The maximum authority available to the agent should be explicitly granted prior to runtime. Additional resources, identities, services, and targets discovered during execution should be treated as outside the authorized boundary unless they are independently validated and added to scope. All authority expansion controls should be implemented outside the AI agent and should not rely solely on system prompts, model alignment, or the agent recognizing that an action is out of scope. These controls do not apply to adversary-controlled AI systems over which the organization has no administrative control. Authority expansion controls include placing restrictions on the number, scope, duration, and concurrent use of authentication and/or authorization tokens available during execution. Tokens may include API access tokens, OAuth tokens, cloud IAM session credentials, service account tokens, Git tokens, or other short-lived authentication artifacts. When policy limits are reached or exceeded, organizations may revoke access, prevent additional token acquisition, require human approval, or terminate the agent's execution. Implementations of these controls may be achieved through enforcement mechanisms such as: - Policy engines - Target allowlists - Protocol and destination restrictions - Approval gates - Preventing the agent from using credentials that were not approved for the task - Monitoring and auditing changes in the agent's effective authority over time Propagate the original authority constraints to sub-agents and delegated tasks. A delegated agent may receive narrower restrictions but should not expand the parent agent's scope, authority, targets, or permitted actions. Authority expansion controls should be implemented alongside permissions configurations for AI agents and tools (See Manage AI Agent Service Access, Manage User-Delegated AI Agent Access, and Enforce Access Controls for AI Agent Tools). Attempted changes in scope should be accompanied with Human In-the-Loop for AI Agent Actions. Log new resource discovery, denials, exceptions, approvals, and scope changes using AI Telemetry Logging and Monitoring.

name: AI Agent Scope Drift Detection
description: Continuously evaluate whether an AI Agent's planned actions remain consistent with its current authorized objective throughout execution. As autonomous agents interact within a dynamic environment, they may discover or generate intermediate objectives or adapt their strategy based on environment feedback. While limited adaption may be necessary to complete legitimate tasks, substantial deviations from the original objective may indicate unintended behavior, excessive autonomy, or attempts to pursue objectives outside the authorized scope. This mitigation does not apply to adversary-controlled AI systems over which the organization has no administrative control. Implementation of scope drift detection can vary through runtime policy engines, planning monitors, orchestration frameworks, or additional supervisory AI Agents. Indicators to monitor may include: - Significant changes in planned objectives or task hierarchy. - Generation of new long-term goals unrelated to the assigned objective. - Tool usage inconsistent with the original mission. - Attempts to access systems or resources outside the authorized scope. - Repeated adaptation toward objectives requiring progressively broader authority. - Planning sequences that introduce persistence, privilege escalation, or unrelated lateral movement. When scope drift is detected, pause execution, restrict tool access, require external human approval, and return the agent to a known authorized plan or terminate the task.

name: AI Honeypots
description: Deploy monitored decoy AI services, agents, credentials, or other resources that resemble legitimate, active assets in the external or internal environment, but serve no real business or operational functions. Because authorized users and workflows have no reason to engage with these resources, any interaction with them is a high-confidence indicator of unauthorized activity such as reconnaissance, or discovery. AI decoys have been shown to surface high-volume reconnaissance and actionable intelligence on threat actors' activities. Positioning honeypot decoys alongside genuine resources helps surface both broad and targeted recon, since an adversary mapping reachable resources in an environment will tend to engage the decoys as well as the real assets. AI decoys that are set up as enticing targets for attackers in different ways can potentially capture how an adversary probes, manipulates, or attempts to abuse them. This can reveal the adversary's intent beyond initial reconnaissance (i.e. what they attempt once engaged), as well as the tactics, techniques and procedures used by the adversary. Interactions with decoy resources can be collected and analyzed to build a threat intelligence feed, capturing adversary source information, tooling, prompts, and techniques. This intelligence can be fed back into detection rules and defenses across the wider environment, while the placed decoys themselves can help confuse and discourage attackers (e.g. by misleading reconnaissance via presenting plausible but false targets), in the goal of wasting the adversary's efforts and resources.

name: Adaptive AI Response Degradation
description: Reduce the utility of AI model outputs for unauthorized model replication, knowledge distillation, or inference about training data by dynamically modifying responses when suspected extraction activity or privacy attacks are detected. Based on the assessed confidence and severity of the activity, apply targeted response modifications that limit the information available to an adversary while preserving legitimate functionality where possible. Response degradation techniques may include: - Routing suspicious requests to less capable or more constrained models - Reducing output precision, specificity, or completeness - Withholding unnecessary reasoning details, confidence information, or auxiliary outputs - Restricting access to high-fidelity or structured responses - Introducing carefully controlled output perturbations These measures can reduce the value of collected responses as training data, limit an adversary's ability to infer model behavior or capabilities, reduce disclosure of information about the model's training data, and increase the cost and difficulty of replicating a target model. Apply response degradation proportionally to the assessed risk of adversarial query activity, using behavioral indicators and detection confidence to minimize disruption to legitimate users. Evaluate degradation mechanisms to ensure they do not introduce misleading or unsafe outputs, inadvertently disclose detection decisions, or undermine the reliability of authorized interactions.

name: Privacy-Preserving AI Training and Inference
description: Use privacy-preserving mechanisms throughout model training and inference to limit disclosure of sensitive training or inference data. These mechanisms can reduce the risk that model outputs reveal sensitive information, such as individual training records, and can also protect sensitive training data from exposure to model developers or operators. Methods that improve privacy in model outputs include Differential Privacy (DP), which provides a formal privacy guarantee limiting how much an individual's data can influence outputs. DP can be applied during training, by adding calibrated noise to clipped gradients, or to inference outputs. Ensuring that models do not overfit during training is also a strategy for limiting model memorization of individual records and improving privacy in deployment. Other privacy-preserving mechanisms can protect data from exposure to developers and operators during training and inference. Federated Learning enables training without revealing training data to training participants. Secure Multi-Party Computation (SMPC) and Homomorphic Encryption can both protect training data from exposure to training participants and also can protect inference inputs from exposure to model operators. These mechanisms by themselves do not prevent disclosure through a deployed model's outputs, but can be combined with DP as a combined strategy.

name: Threat Intelligence Program
description: A Threat Intelligence Program enables organizations to proactively collect, analyze, and share information on threats to AI and cyber systems by leveraging internal observations and external reporting. The program supports decision-making processes, prioritizes defenses, and improves incident response by delivering actionable intelligence tailored to the organization's risk profile and operational environment. This mitigation can be implemented through the following measures: **Establish an AI Threat Intelligence Team and Define and Requirements** - Assign personnel to collect, analyze, and act on intelligence related to threats targeting AI systems. - Coordinate across cybersecurity, AI/ML development, and model evaluation teams to translate intelligence into actionable defenses. - Define intelligence requirements around critical AI assets, dependencies, deployment environments, and the decisions intelligence must support. - Prioritize collection according to relevant adversary objectives, capabilities, access requirements, and potential operational impacts. Include threats to AI components and the software, services, and infrastructure supporting them. **Collect and Automate AI Threat Intelligence** - Collect intelligence from internal sources, including AI application logs, model monitoring, red-team exercises, security incidents, and adversarial testing. - Monitor external sources, including AI vulnerability disclosures, incident reports, security research, and threat intelligence feeds. - Track active campaigns and adversary capabilities, including autonomous agent campaigns, reported use of zero-day vulnerabilities, and impersonation campaigns. - Collect information on compromised supply chains and published poisoned datasets, models, and AI agent tools. - Use threat intelligence platforms (TIPs) to aggregate, enrich, and disseminate AI-related threat intelligence. - Integrate intelligence with SIEMs and AI monitoring tools to correlate indicators of compromise with internal events. **Analyze and Operationalize Intelligence** - Map emerging and observed threats to MITRE ATLAS tactics and techniques to understand adversary behaviors and potential impacts. - Assess applicability to deployed components, versions, configurations, and workflows, including the access and conditions required for an attack. - Prioritize defensive actions based on threat relevance, AI system criticality, and potential operational impact. - Use intelligence to identify affected systems and artifacts, prioritize remediation or compensating controls, and update threat models, adversarial evaluations, detection logic, and incident response procedures. - Correlate relevant indicators and behaviors with internal telemetry to identify related activity. Validate detection logic against the organization's environment and available observations. - Assign defensive actions to responsible owners, track their completion, and verify whether they address the identified exposure. **Share Intelligence and Continuously Improve** - Share AI threat intelligence, attack patterns, and lessons learned with trusted industry partners and AI security communities. - Regularly update intelligence priorities as AI capabilities, vulnerabilities, and adversarial techniques evolve. - Evaluate program effectiveness based on improvements in threat detection, defensive coverage, and incident re sponse. **Tools and Resources for Implementation** - Threat Knowledge Bases and Intelligence Sources - MITRE ATLAS: Organize intelligence around documented adversary behaviors. - Vendor advisories, CVE/NVD, and CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog: Identify vulnerabilities affecting deployed components. - Supplier and repository security reporting: Identify compromised models, datasets, packages, containers, and AI agent tools. - Incident reports and security research: Assess targeting and attack methods, distinguishing operational activity from research demonstrations. - Intelligence Management and Sharing - Threat intelligence platforms, such as OpenCTI and MISP: Organize and share indicators, relationships, sources, and confidence assessments. - STIX and TAXII: Support structured intelligence exchange between compatible systems. - Case-management systems: Track investigations, assigned defensive actions, and outcomes. - Operational Analysis and Validation - SIEMs and AI monitoring tools: Correlate intelligence with internal telemetry to investigate related activity. - Asset and dependency inventories: Identify exposure to reported vulnerabilities and compromised artifacts. - Security evaluation capabilities: Turn intelligence into system-specific tests using appropriate manual and automated methods. - Community and Collaboration - ISACs and AI security communities: Exchange relevant campaign observations and defensive findings. - Supplier and platform reporting channels: Report malicious artifacts and compromised services to support investigation and removal.

name: AI Agent External Resource Lifecycle Management
description: Organizations should control external resources created or acquired by AI agents during execution by treating those resources as attributable, lifecycle-managed assets. These resources may remain usable after the originating agent's environment has been destroyed, allowing unauthorized activity to persist across otherwise ephemeral sessions, and enabling discovery and reuse by other agents. External resources may include identities and access mechanisms, compute, storage and network infrastructure, hosted data, model artifacts, installed software, and externally maintained services and integrations. Where possible, agents should create such resources through a broker or management layer that records resource identifiers, ownership, purpose, creation time, authorized scope, and expiration or approved retention conditions. Resources should be issued with the shortest practical lifetime consistent with their authorized purpose and tied to the specific agent run, task, user, or operational objective that required them. Define expiration or retention conditions at provisioning time and require explicit authorization to extend resource lifetimes or transfer ownership. Enforce these controls outside the agent and restrict provisioning paths that bypass registration or lifecycle controls. When the authorized need ends or authorization expires, all lifecycle-managed resources that are no longer required should be cleaned up. This includes revoking associated credentials, disabling or deleting accounts, removing hosted artifacts, and tearing down external infrastructure. Cleanup mechanisms should operate independently of the agent's execution environment, with periodic inventory reconciliation to detect residual resources and retry failed cleanup. Verify credential revocation and resource removal separately, since revoking credentials does not necessarily disable resources created using them. Where deletion is impossible or delayed, revoke access and isolate residual resources. Retained resources should be assigned to a new owner with an approved lifecycle policy.
